paraphrase: Gautama asks how knowledge of Brahman arises; Sanatsujāta answers with the teaching Śiva gave Pārvatī after examining all the Vedas, a secret for yogins that gives enjoyment and liberation.
speaker: Sanatsujāta

paraphrase: The haṃsa, repeating 'haṃsa haṃsa', pervades all bodies as fire in wood and oil in sesame; knowing it one passes beyond death. The teaching is for the celibate, calm, restrained student devoted to the guru.

Pressing the anus and raising the breath from the ādhāra, the yogin circles the svādhiṣṭhāna, passes the maṇipūra, anāhata, viśuddhi and ājñā and meditates at the brahmarandhra: 'I am the three-measured one'; thus he sees and becomes formless.
The haṃsa mantra has haṃsa as seer, avyakta-gāyatrī as metre and paramahaṃsa as deity; ham is its seed, sa its power, so'ham its bolt; it is repeated 21,600 times a day with every breath.
The haṃsa is visualized as a bird: fire and moon its wings, oṃkāra its head, bindu its eye.

In the eight-petalled heart lotus the mind's disposition follows the petal it rests on — east virtue, south-east sleep and sloth, south cruelty, south-west sin, west play, north-west going and moving, north love, north-east giving; at the centre dispassion; filaments waking, pericarp dream, liṅga deep sleep; leaving the lotus, the fourth; when the haṃsa is absorbed in nāda, the state beyond the fourth (unmanī).
After much japa the nāda is heard in ten forms: ciṇī, ciñciṇī, bell, conch, lute, cymbal, flute, mṛdaṅga drum, bherī drum and thunder-cloud; the yogin abandons the first nine and practises the tenth.

Effects follow the sounds in order: tingling, the limbs 'breaking', fatigue, head shaking, the palate dripping, drinking nectar, secret knowledge, the supreme speech, the body becoming invisible with the divine eye, and with the tenth he becomes Brahman — where mind dissolves, merit and sin are burnt, and the Self shines as Sadāśiva.
Mind is said to be of two kinds, pure and impure: impure when joined with desire, pure when free of desire.
Mind alone is the cause of human bondage and liberation: attached to objects it leads to bondage, free of objects to liberation.

original.text: mana eva manuṣyāṇāṃ kāraṇaṃ bandhamokṣayoḥ | bandhāya viṣayāsaktaṃ muktyai nirviṣayaṃ smṛtam

paraphrase: When the mind, free of attachment and restrained in the heart, becomes non-existent (unmanībhāva), that is the supreme state; it should be restrained until it perishes in the heart — this is knowledge and meditation, the rest is extension of books.
There is no dissolution, no origination, no one bound, no seeker, no aspirant for liberation and none liberated — this is the highest truth.

The one Self abides in waking, dream and deep sleep; the one being-self appears many in beings like the moon in water; as space in a pot is not destroyed when the pot breaks, the Self is not destroyed with the body.

Two Brahmans are to be known, the word-Brahman and the supreme; one versed in the word-Brahman reaches the supreme. Having studied the books, the wise one devoted to knowledge should cast them away like husk after taking the grain.

Knowledge is hidden in every being like ghee in milk; it is to be churned with the mind as churning rod. The knower concludes: 'I am Vāsudeva', the partless, stainless Brahman in whom all beings dwell.
Having studied the scriptures and reflected on them again and again, the wise one who has known Brahman should abandon them like a torch after the goal is seen.
Mounting the chariot of Oṃ with Viṣṇu as charioteer, one goes to Rudra's world; as far as the chariot goes, then leaving it one reaches the place beyond.
Withdrawal, meditation, breath-control, concentration, reasoning (tarka) and absorption — this is called the six-limbed yoga.
As impurities of ore are burnt by blowing, so faults born of the senses are burnt by restraining breath; sins by breath-control, faults by concentration, and so on.
Like one blind, deaf and like a piece of wood, the yogin should abide unmoved (in practice).
Tarka (the fifth limb) is reasoning not opposed to the āgamas; samādhi is that by which, when it is attained, one regards everything as equal.
Seated in the lotus, svastika or bhadra posture, facing north, the yogin closes one nostril and draws breath through the other; he should meditate on Oṃ.
The yogin should abandon fear, anger, sloth, too much sleep and too much waking, too much food and fasting.
If the rule is kept well, knowledge arises in three months; in four he sees the gods, in five he gains power equal to theirs, and in six he attains kaivalya.
Breathing goes on 1,13,680 times a day and night; prāṇa dwells in the heart, apāna in the anus, samāna in the navel, udāna in the throat, vyāna throughout the body; each has its colour.
One who breaks through (the bonds) with breath going out through the crown does not return to birth.

The Kṣurikā ('razor') teaches a concentration (dhāraṇā) by which the mind, joined with breath, cuts through the vital points of the body from the feet upward and all the channels except the suṣumnā; with the razor of mind sharpened on the stone of dispassion the yogin severs the bonds of rebirth. Recorded as a summary only; no steps.

One should meditate on the 'point of light' (tejobindu), subtle and beyond the senses, hard to see and reach; it is for the one who has conquered food, anger, association, the senses and the pairs of opposites.
The limbs are fifteen: yama, niyama, tyāga, mauna, deśa, kāla, āsana, mūlabandha, dehasāmya, dṛksthiti, prāṇasaṃyamana, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, ātmadhyāna and samādhi.

Each limb is knowledge: yama is restraint of the senses by the knowledge 'all is Brahman'; niyama the flow of like thoughts; silence is not mere silence of speech (that is for children); the true seat is where Brahman-contemplation flows; the true root-lock is Brahman, root of the worlds; evenness of body is dissolving in the even Brahman, not the straightness of a dry tree; the true gaze is seeing the world as Brahman, not looking at the nose-tip; prāṇāyāma is stopping all modifications by seeing all as Brahman — negating the world is exhalation, 'I am Brahman' inhalation, steadiness retention.
This (inner prāṇāyāma) is for the awakened; pressing the nose is for the ignorant.

In practising samādhi obstacles arise: lack of inquiry, sloth, desire for enjoyment, dissolution (laya), darkness, distraction, radiance (tejas), sweating and blankness; the knower of Brahman should avoid them.

By thinking of an existent one becomes it, by thinking of the void, void; by the thought of Brahman, fullness; those who merely talk of Brahman without that inner state, attached to pleasure, are born again and again.
Kumāra asks Śiva about the partless, single-flavoured pure consciousness; Śiva teaches that everything — self, world, teacher, scripture — is that consciousness alone.
speaker: Śiva

paraphrase: Kumāra asks about the one liberated in life and the one liberated without body: the jīvanmukta abides as pure consciousness, free of 'I' and 'mine', while the body continues; the videhamukta is Brahman without remainder.
Nidāgha asks Ṛbhu to teach discrimination of self and not-self; Ṛbhu teaches that the Self is beyond the three states, bodies and sheaths, and all else is not-self and unreal.
Oṃ is a bird: a is its right wing, u its left, m its tail, and the half-measure its head.

The twelve measures (ghoṣiṇī, vidyunmātrā, pataṅginī, vāyuveginī, nāmadheyā, aindrī, vaiṣṇavī, śāṅkarī, mahatī, dhṛti, nārī, brāhmī) each give a destiny to one who dies in it — from a universal king, yakṣa, vidyādhara and gandharva, to the worlds of Soma, Indra, Viṣṇu and Rudra, the Mahar, Jana and Tapas worlds, and in the last, the eternal Brahman.

For the knower, prārabdha karma is not destroyed by knowledge alone but its hold is like the objects of a dream on one who has woken; as the snake seen in a rope, the body and world are superimposed; knowledge destroys accumulated and future karma.
Seated in siddhāsana, holding the vaiṣṇavī mudrā, the yogin should always listen to the inner sound in the right ear.
At first the sounds are loud — like the ocean, clouds, kettledrum and waterfall; in the middle, like the mardala drum, bell and horn; at the end, like tinkling bells, flute, vīṇā and bee.
Hearing the subtler sound within the loud, the mind fixed on it does not wander; it becomes one with nāda like milk mixed with water and quickly dissolves in the space of consciousness.

As the bee drinking honey does not care for fragrance, the mind absorbed in nāda does not crave objects; nāda is the charm that stills the snake of the mind, the goad for the elephant of mind, the net for the deer of mind, the shore for the ocean of mind.
The sound lasts only while there is space; the soundless is the supreme Brahman, the supreme Self. As long as there is sound there is mind; the end of sound is the state beyond mind (manonmanī).

The yogin absorbed in nāda lies like a dead man, his body like a log, unaware of heat and cold, pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour; his gaze, breath and mind are steady without support — he is liberated.
Even if sin were piled high as a mountain many yojanas wide, it is destroyed by the yoga of meditation, and by nothing else ever.
Oṃ's letters correspond to Vedas, worlds and deities; a is yellow and of rajas, u white and of sattva, m black and of tamas.
Oṃ is the bow, the self the arrow, Brahman the target; it is to be pierced by the heedful (quoting Muṇḍaka).
Meditate on Oṃ as the thumb-sized Lord in the heart; Brahmā is inhalation, Viṣṇu retention, Rudra exhalation.
Posture, breath-restraint, withdrawal, concentration, meditation and absorption are the six limbs. There are as many postures as beings; four are named — siddha, bhadra, siṃha and padma.

The body's centres: the ādhāra with four petals and the triangle (yoni) and liṅga; the svādhiṣṭhāna; the maṇipūra, a twelve-spoked wheel where the jīva wanders driven by merit and sin; the kanda from which 72,000 channels spread, ten of them principal (iḍā, piṅgalā, suṣumnā, gāndhārī, hastijihvā, pūṣā, yaśasvinī, alambusā, kuhū, śaṅkhinī).
The jīva, moved by prāṇa and apāna, goes up and down, never resting, like a ball struck by the hand, or a bird tied by a string that flies off and is pulled back.
The jīva goes out with the sound ha and returns with sa, repeating 'haṃsa' 21,600 times a day; this ajapā-gāyatrī gives liberation to yogins; knowing it one is freed from sin.

The kuṇḍalinī sleeps covering with her mouth the door to Brahman; awakened by fire, mind and breath, she rises through the suṣumnā like a needle drawing thread; the yogin opens the door of liberation with her as a key opens a door.
Khecarī mudrā and the retention of bindu are described: bindu is twofold, white (śukla, Śiva) and red (rajas, Śakti), and their union in the body is the yogin's aim. Recorded as a summary only.

In the heart lotus the moods follow the petals: east (white) dharma, south-east (red) sleep and sloth, south (black) hatred, south-west (blue) sin and violence, west (crystal) play, north-west (ruby) going and dispassion, north (yellow) pleasure, north-east (lapis) charity; at the junctions, disease; at the centre, knowing all.
Resting in the successive circles of the lotus the self experiences waking, dream, deep sleep, the fourth and what is beyond the fourth.
When the nāda is heard and the Self is seen in the cavity of the skull, the yogin attains kaivalya.
Oṃ's body: a is the Ṛgveda, the gārhapatya fire, the earth and Brahmā; u the Yajurveda, the dakṣiṇa fire, the mid-space and Viṣṇu; m the Sāmaveda, the āhavanīya fire, the sky and Īśvara.
Like the sound of a bell fading into peace, the praṇava's end is to be meditated on; it leads to the supreme.
The jīva repeats the haṃsa with every breath (sa going in, ha going out); haṃsa-vidyā is the only means to liberation.
The disciple should do whatever the guru says without deliberating; then, having gained knowledge, he may abandon caste, stage of life and even the Vedas like dust; the guru is Hari himself.
Three kinds of teacher: the codaka who points out the path, the bodhaka who shows the place, and the mokṣada who gives the supreme; addressed to Gautama.
By this practice the three knots (Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra) are pierced.
A long litany of self-knowledge: 'I am the witness, the pure, the partless; I am Brahman' — the knower's declarations.
Brahmā (Pitāmaha) asks Viṣṇu (Hṛṣīkeśa) about the essence of yoga; Viṣṇu teaches it.
speaker: Viṣṇu

paraphrase: The jīva is bound by twenty faults — desire, anger, fear, delusion, greed, pride, passion, birth, death, miserliness, grief, drowsiness, hunger, thirst, craving, shame, fright, sorrow, dejection and elation; free of them, it is called Śiva.
How can knowledge without yoga give liberation? Yoga without knowledge is also incapable of it; the seeker should firmly practise both knowledge and yoga.

paraphrase: Saṃsāra comes from ignorance alone, and liberation from knowledge alone.
Yoga, though one, is divided in practice into mantra-yoga, laya-yoga, haṭha-yoga and rāja-yoga; its stages everywhere are four: ārambha, ghaṭa, paricaya and niṣpatti.

paraphrase: Mantra-yoga — repeating a mantra with the letters of the alphabet for twelve years — gradually gives knowledge and powers; it is for the dullest practitioner.
Laya-yoga is dissolving the mind: meditating on the partless Lord while walking, standing, sleeping or eating.
Haṭha-yoga has eight limbs (yama to samādhi) and uses mahāmudrā, mahābandha, khecarī, the three bandhas, and vajrolī, amarolī and sahajolī (the last three recorded by name only).
Light and moderate food is the chief of the yamas, non-injury the chief of the niyamas; the chief postures are four: siddha, padma, siṃha and bhadra.
Obstacles arise at first: sloth, boasting, the company of rogues, pursuit of mantras and the like, and craving for metals and women — all mirages; the wise should abandon them.
The yogin should live in a well-built, secluded hut (maṭha), clean, free of insects, and practise there.
Purification of the channels by alternate-nostril breathing is taught in regular sessions; the counts and schedules given in the text are not reproduced here.

Signs after purification: lightness, radiance, strong digestive fire, leanness. The practitioner should avoid salt, mustard, sour, hot and pungent food, fire, women, travel, early bathing, fasting and mortifying the body; milk, ghee, wheat, mung and rice are wholesome.
When kevala-kumbhaka arises spontaneously the signs follow: sweating, trembling, frog-like hopping and rising from the ground; less excreta and sleep. He should not display these powers.
The yogin becomes attractive to women; union with them causes loss of bindu, so he should avoid their company.
In the ghaṭa stage prāṇa and apāna, mind and intellect, jīvātman and paramātman become one.
Pratyāhāra: whatever one sees, hears, smells, tastes or touches, one should regard as the Self.

Powers arise — far-hearing, far-seeing, going great distances, command of speech, taking forms at will, invisibility, turning iron to gold with his excreta, moving in the sky. These are obstacles to the great attainment; the wise yogin never delights in them and hides them, living as if a fool, blind or deaf.
Disciples will ask for favours out of self-interest; the yogin busied with them forgets his practice; he should remember the guru's words day and night.

Five element-concentrations: earth (feet to knees, square, yellow, la, Brahmā), water (knees to anus, half-moon, white, va, Nārāyaṇa), fire (anus to heart, triangle, red, ra, Rudra), air (heart to brows, hexagon, black, ya, Īśvara), space (brows to crown, circle, smoky, ha, Sadāśiva); each conquers its element. Durations omitted.

Meditation with and without qualities leads to samādhi, in which the jīva and the supreme are the same; the yogin may then leave the body at will or roam the worlds with powers; the difference is in the practice, the fruit is the same.

Mahābandha, mahāvedha, khecarī, the three bandhas, viparītakaraṇī (with the warning that the yogin must then eat well, or the fire consumes the body), vajrolī and amarolī are described; recorded summary-only.
Rāja-yoga follows, giving discrimination and dispassion.
The wheel of births: the mother of one life becomes the wife of another, the father the son; like buckets on a water-wheel beings go up and down through wombs.
Oṃ comprises the three worlds, Vedas, times, fires and deities; the half-measure beyond is the supreme; meditate on it.
As a tortoise draws in its limbs, the yogin withdraws the senses; like a lamp in a pot, the Self shines within; meditate on it as the unwavering flame.
The brāhmaṇa Triśikhi goes to Āditya's world and asks what the body is, what the life-breath, what the cause and what the Self; the Sun answers: all is Śiva.
From yoga comes knowledge and from knowledge yoga; yoga is twofold — of knowledge and of action; the yogin established in both never perishes.

In the yoga of knowledge the limbs are redefined: yama is dispassion toward body and senses; niyama constant attachment to the supreme; āsana indifference to all things; prāṇāyāma knowing the world as unreal; pratyāhāra turning the mind inward; dhāraṇā motionless mind; dhyāna 'I am pure consciousness'; samādhi the forgetting of meditation.

Ten yamas — non-injury, truth, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion, rectitude, forbearance, fortitude, moderate diet, purity; ten niyamas — austerity, contentment, faith, charity, worship of Hari, hearing Vedānta, modesty, discernment (mati), japa, vows.

Seventeen postures are described — svastika, gomukha, vīra, yoga, padma, baddhapadma, kukkuṭa, uttāna-kūrma, dhanur, siṃha, bhadra, mukta, mayūra, matsya, siddha, paścimatāna and sukha; conquering posture conquers the three worlds.

The body is ninety-six digits; the fire-centre has a different shape in each species; at the navel is a twelve-spoked wheel ('I turn it by my māyā'), where the jīva moves like a spider in its web; kuṇḍalī lies coiled eightfold; the channels spread from the kanda.

The ten vital winds and their functions: prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, vyāna; nāga for belching, kūrma for blinking, kṛkara for sneezing and hunger, devadatta for sleep and yawning, dhanañjaya which does not leave even the corpse.
Prāṇāyāma has three grades: the lowest produces sweat, the middle trembling, the highest rising of the body.
Omens of death: when throbbing ceases in certain places of the limbs the remaining life is a year, six months, three months and so on; not seeing the tip of one's tongue, a few days.
Pratyāhāra: holding the breath successively at eighteen vital points (marma) of the body, from the toes upward, and back.
Element-concentrations with the vyūha deities: earth with Aniruddha, water with Nārāyaṇa, fire with Pradyumna, air with Saṅkarṣaṇa, space with Vāsudeva.
The states are placed in the body: waking between navel and heart, dream in the throat, deep sleep in the palate, the fourth between the brows, the beyond-fourth in the brahmarandhra.
Samādhi is the knowledge 'I am the supreme Brahman'; the yogin becomes Brahman.

Posture, breath-restraint, withdrawal, concentration, meditation and absorption are the six limbs of yoga; of postures siddha and kamala (lotus) are chief. The yogin should know the six centres, sixteen supports (ādhāra), three targets (lakṣya) and five voids (vyoma).
The jīva is tossed up and down by prāṇa and apāna like a ball struck by the bat, and like a hawk tied by a string it is drawn back.
The jīva repeats the ajapā-gāyatrī 21,600 times a day; it arises from the kuṇḍalinī; it is the knowledge of prāṇa and the great knowledge.
Moderate diet is food that is sweet and unctuous, leaving a quarter of the stomach empty, eaten for Śiva's pleasure. The kuṇḍalinī is bondage for the ignorant and liberation for yogins.

Praṇava and the four states; sa means 'you' and ha 'that' — their union is 'that you are'; bound by the senses and 'mine' one is jīva, by 'not mine' kevala; one who repeats the praṇava, pure or impure, is untouched like a lotus leaf by water.
Signs of purified channels: breath held at will, stronger digestive fire, the inner sound manifest, and health.
Posture destroys disease, prāṇāyāma sin, pratyāhāra mental disturbance; dhāraṇā gives steadiness of mind, samādhi the wonderful consciousness and liberation.
Twelve prāṇāyāmas make a pratyāhāra, twelve pratyāhāras a dhāraṇā, twelve dhāraṇās a dhyāna, twelve dhyānas a samādhi.
Closing the senses (the ṣaṇmukhī) the yogin hears sounds like bells within.

Proper prāṇāyāma destroys all disease; improper practice produces hiccup, asthma, cough, pains of head, ears and eyes. As a lion, elephant or tiger is tamed slowly, breath must be controlled gradually, otherwise it kills the practitioner.
Yājñavalkya goes to the solar world and asks the Person there about the Self; Nārāyaṇa teaches the eight-limbed yoga joined with knowledge.

Yama: conquering cold, heat, food and sleep, calm, steadiness and sense-restraint; niyama: devotion to the guru, love of the path of truth, enjoying what comes unsought, contentment, non-attachment, solitude, cessation of mind, no desire for fruits, dispassion; a comfortable posture; breath-control; withdrawal; dhyāna is one-pointedness on the consciousness in all bodies; samādhi is the forgetting of meditation.
The body has five faults — desire, anger, (disturbed) breathing, fear and sleep; their remedies are freedom from willing, forbearance, light food, vigilance and devotion to truth.
To cross the ocean of saṃsāra whose waves are sleep and fear, one takes the subtle path, meditating on the tāraka light between the brows, with the three targets.
Tāraka is twofold — the earlier tāraka and the later amanaska; tāraka with form and without; śāmbhavī, the gaze on the inner target with eyes open, is secret in all the tantras.

Views of the inner target differ — water-like light in the thousand-petalled lotus; the person in the cave of the intellect; the five-faced blue-throated Lord with Umā; the thumb-sized person — all these are the Self alone.

The gaze has three forms — amā (eyes closed), pratipat (half open) and pūrṇimā (open) — and the full-moon gaze is to be practised; signs follow: a star, a diamond mirror, the full moon, nine gems, the midday sun, a flame.
Lights appear in the west — crystal, smoke, bindu, nāda, kalā, stars, fireflies, lamps, eyes, gold, gems; they are the form of the praṇava.
For one who has seen, there are no rites, since the sun of consciousness neither rises nor sets.

Worship is mapped onto the state beyond mind: meditation is absence of thought; invocation abandoning action; the seat firm knowledge; water for the feet the unmanī state; the offering the amanaska state; the bath radiance; perfume seeing all; the lamp the sun of consciousness; salutation 'so'ham'; praise silence; dismissal total contentment.
Deep sleep and samādhi both dissolve the mind, yet differ: in sleep mind dissolves in tamas and it is not the cause of liberation; in samādhi the world dissolves into the witness-consciousness.
The five states — waking, dream, deep sleep, the fourth and beyond the fourth; mind with intention is bondage.
Amanaska: the mind becomes like an udder after milking; 'you are I, I am you'; the guru embraces the disciple and imparts the knowledge.

The five voids: ākāśa (dark within and without), parākāśa (like the fire of dissolution), mahākāśa (immeasurable light), sūryākāśa (like the sun) and paramākāśa (indescribable, blissful). 'One who does not know the nine cakras, six supports, three targets and five voids is a yogin in name only.'

When the anāhata sound is heard, its resonance becomes light and the mind dissolves there — the supreme state of Viṣṇu; the knower behaves like a child, madman or goblin; he is a paramahaṃsa avadhūta whose sight purifies the world and who saves a hundred and one generations.
This teaching is for the renouncer who has conquered the senses and is endowed with the six qualities (calm and the rest).
Tāraka is so called because it makes one cross the great fear of birth, old age and death; by 'not this, not this' one knows the Self as distinct from the body.

Three targets: the inner (the kuṇḍalinī in the suṣumnā; the sound heard on closing the ears; a blue light between the eyes), the outer (colours of space seen at distances in front of the nose, rays and a light above the head), and the intermediate (a sequence of voids).

In the intermediate target the yogin sees in turn the space without qualities, the supreme space like dense darkness lit by stars, the great space like the fire of dissolution, the space of principles, and the space of the sun like crores of suns.
Śāmbhavī mudrā is the gaze on the inner target while the eyes look outward without blinking; the place where such a yogin lives is purified.

The true teacher knows the Vedas, is devoted to Viṣṇu, free of envy, a yogin devoted to his own guru, who knows the Person. 'Gu' is darkness and 'ru' its remover: because he removes darkness he is called guru; the guru is the supreme Brahman.

paraphrase: Brahmā teaches that this knowledge is not to be given to the unqualified; ignorance is darkness — the body and world — and knowledge is the sun's orb.
'That sun is Brahman': meditating with the ajapā 'haṃsaḥ so'ham' one sees the self-luminous consciousness.
This is not samādhi, not attainment of yoga, not dissolution of mind — it is oneness with Brahman.
Mind has two causes, vāsanā and breath; when one is destroyed both are destroyed.
Of these, the breath is conquered by moderate diet, posture and the moving of the power (śakticālana).
Śakticālana — moving the kuṇḍalī from her place toward the brows — and sarasvatī-cālana are described; the text says they cure abdominal diseases. Recorded summary-only.
Kumbhaka is twofold, sahita and kevala; sahita is of four kinds: sūrya(bheda), ujjāyī, śītalī and bhastrī. Methods and counts are not reproduced here.
The three bandhas — mūla, uḍḍīyāna and jālandhara — are to be practised.

Disease arises from sleeping by day, keeping awake at night, excess of sex, crowds, suppressing the urges, unwholesome food and strain; the diseased practitioner then gives up yoga, thinking it caused the illness — this is the first obstacle.

Ten obstacles: disease, doubt, heedlessness, sloth, sleep, withdrawal of interest, delusion, and further obstacles (readings uncertain) ending with failure to attain the truth of yoga; the wise should overcome them.

The kuṇḍalinī, roused like a serpent struck with a stick, enters the suṣumnā, pierces the knots of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra and the six lotuses, and unites with Śiva in the thousand-petalled lotus; then the world is seen to arise and dissolve falsely, like silver in mother-of-pearl.
The khecarī-vidyā is to be learnt from a guru who knows it from text, meaning and practice; its mantra (melana) comes only from the guru's mouth; it must be kept secret.

Bodily procedures of khecarī are described; they are not reproduced here. The text warns that they must be done gradually, never all at once, or the body perishes, and gives a long period of practice.
Mind is bindu, the cause of creation and preservation; as milk becomes ghee, so is bindu.
Six centres: mūlādhāra at the anus, svādhiṣṭhāna at the genitals, maṇipūra at the navel, anāhata at the heart, viśuddhi at the throat, ājñā in the head.
Fire hidden in wood appears only by churning; a lamp in a pot shows only when the pot breaks — the guru's word breaks it; the guru is the helmsman across saṃsāra.
Speech sprouts in parā, puts forth two leaves in paśyantī, buds in madhyamā and blossoms in vaikharī; by reversing this order sound is dissolved.
One established in 'so'ham asmi' ('I am He') is untouched by any words, good or bad.
Self-inquiry: 'Who am I? How did this world arise?' — one should inquire in this way.
Such a one is liberated while living; when the body falls he attains bodiless liberation, like the wind becoming still.
Dattātreya, the four-armed Mahāviṣṇu, teaches his disciple Sāṅkṛti the eight-limbed yoga.

Ten yamas are defined twice over — outwardly and inwardly: non-injury is not harming (except as the Veda enjoins), and supremely, knowing the Self as all-pervading; truth is speech that is true, and supremely 'all is Brahman'; purity is external, and inward as 'I am pure'.
The body is utterly impure, the embodied Self utterly pure; one who abandons the purity of knowledge for external purity abandons gold for a clod.

Ten niyamas (austerity, contentment, faith, charity, worship of the Lord, hearing the settled doctrine, modesty, discernment, japa, vows); worship of the Lord is a heart free of passion, speech free of falsehood, action free of violence; japa is spoken (loud or whispered) or mental, the whispered worth a thousand loud, the mental a thousand whispered.
Nine postures — svastika, gomukha, padma, vīra, siṃha, bhadra, mukta, mayūra and sukha.
Fourteen channels are principal; the suṣumnā, the brahma-nāḍī along the spine (vīṇādaṇḍa), is chief; the kuṇḍalī lies below.
Deities of the channels: suṣumnā Śiva, iḍā Hari, piṅgalā Brahmā, and others.

Time within the body: the moon moves in iḍā, the sun in piṅgalā; passage from piṅgalā to iḍā is the northern course, the reverse the southern; their junction is the new moon; the mūlādhāra and the head are the equinoxes; the eclipses happen within.

The sacred places are in the body — Śrīparvata in the head, Kedāra on the forehead, Vārāṇasī between brows and nose, Kurukṣetra in the breast, Prayāga in the heart lotus, Cidambaram in the heart; one who leaves the inner tīrtha for the outer throws away a gem for glass; an impure mind is not cleansed by bathing, as a liquor pot is not by washing. Yogins see Śiva in the Self, not in images; images are imagined for the ignorant.
Channels are purified by breath practice, with signs of lightness, digestive fire and inner sound; or the yogin may purify himself by the knowledge of the Self.
Prāṇāyāma with the measures of a, u and m; grades of sweat, trembling and rising.
Sounds of the conch, thunder and waterfall are heard in the brahmarandhra; by dispassion knowledge arises.

Five pratyāhāras: forcibly withdrawing the senses; seeing all that is seen as the Self; offering all acts' fruits to Brahman; doing daily and occasional rites as worship of Brahman; and moving the breath through eighteen vital points and fixing it there, the self in the Self.

Dhāraṇā: dissolving the outer elements into their places in the body with their syllables and deities — Brahmā earth, Viṣṇu water, Maheśa fire, Īśvara air, Sadāśiva space — or holding Śiva as the Person.
Dhyāna: 'so'ham' — meditating on Maheśvara as oneself, 'I am' as being-consciousness-bliss.

Samādhi is the knowledge of the unity of jīva and the supreme; the Self appears divided only through māyā; 'I am not the body… I am Śiva alone'; seeing all beings in the Self, Sāṅkṛti abides fearless.
Atharvan tells Śāṇḍilya: there are eight limbs — ten yamas, ten niyamas, eight postures, three prāṇāyāmas, five pratyāhāras, dhāraṇā, two kinds of dhyāna and one samādhi.
Non-injury is causing no pain to any being by mind, speech or body; truth is speaking what is true and beneficial; … purity is external (earth and water) and internal (by knowledge of the Self).

Niyamas: worship of the Lord is worshipping Viṣṇu, Rudra and the others with a clear mind; hearing the doctrine is inquiring into Vedānta; japa is loud, whispered (a thousand times better) or mental (a crore times better).
Fourteen principal channels; the suṣumnā is the path to liberation; the moon (tamas, nectar) moves in iḍā, the sun (rajas, poison) in piṅgalā; suṣumnā devours time.
The qualified practitioner lives in a hermitage, worships Vināyaka and his chosen deity, and purifies the channels.
Praṇava is prāṇāyāma; a is Gāyatrī (red, on a swan, a girl), u Sāvitrī (white, on Garuḍa, youthful), m Sarasvatī (black, on a bull, aged).
As a lion, elephant or tiger is tamed gradually, so breath is to be controlled; otherwise it kills the practitioner.
When kevala-kumbhaka is mastered the kuṇḍalinī awakens and the suṣumnā is freed of obstruction; signs appear. Method not reproduced.
Vaiṣṇavī mudrā: the target within, the gaze outward without blinking — secret in all tantras.
There are two ways of destroying the mind: yoga, the stopping of its modifications, and knowledge, right seeing; for some yoga is impossible, for others knowledge.

Ways of stilling the vibration of prāṇa (shared with the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha): study, association with the wise, dispassion, practice, fixing on one object, restraint of breath, meditation on the heart-space, and others.
The kuṇḍalinī rising above the throat gives liberation to yogins; remaining below it binds the ignorant.

Saṃyama on parts and principles gives powers: on the body's parts knowledge of the worlds; on merit and demerit knowledge of past and future; on the throat freedom from hunger; on the kūrma-nāḍī steadiness; on the light in the head vision of siddhas; and others.

Five pratyāhāras: forcibly withdrawing the senses; seeing all as the Self; renouncing the fruits of daily acts; turning from all objects; and holding (the breath) at the eighteen vital points in ascending and descending order.

Dhāraṇā is threefold (fixing mind in the Self, outer space in the heart-space, the five deities in the elements); dhyāna is with qualities (form) or without (the Self's nature); samādhi is the union of jīvātman and paramātman free from the triad.
Śāṇḍilya, not finding brahmavidyā in the four Vedas, asks Atharvan; Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite, and 'that you are'.

Brahman has three forms — with parts, without parts, and with-and-without parts; its most manifest form is Dattātreya, who gave himself to Atri and was born of Anasūyā; his meditation form is the naked avadhūta smeared with ash.
Ṛbhu performs austerity for twelve divine years; the Lord appears as Varāha and offers a boon; Ṛbhu asks for the knowledge that frees from saṃsāra.

The principles are counted as 24, 36 or 96; the ninety-six add to the 24 the five elements, three bodies, three states, six modifications, six waves (hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, old age, death), six sheaths, six enemies, three jīvas, three guṇas, three karmas, five actions, four inner functions, the four sublime attitudes (friendliness, compassion, joy, equanimity) and fourteen deities.
Worshippers of Varāha become liberated while living; those who know the ninety-six are freed in any stage of life, whether matted, shaven or with topknot.
The fourfold means (discrimination, dispassion, the six virtues, desire for liberation) come by one's dharma of caste and stage, austerity and pleasing the guru.
True fasting (upavāsa) is 'dwelling near' — the jīva abiding with the supreme Self — not drying up the body; beating the anthill does not kill the snake.
'Brahman is' is indirect knowledge; 'I am Brahman' is direct; the knower is liberated while living from the moment of knowing.
Renouncing objects, seeing the truth, and the natural state are hard to gain without the grace of a true guru.
An analogy between mercury and mind (both are fixed by the right means) is given; no procedure for mercury is recorded here.
Mind is lord of the senses, breath lord of the mind, and dissolution (laya) lord of the breath.
The ignorant seek powers through substances, mantras, rites and times; the knower does not, for powers do not lead to the supreme.

Nidāgha asks about the stages; Ṛbhu teaches seven: good desire (śubhecchā), inquiry (vicāraṇā), thinning of mind (tanumānasī), attainment of sattva (sattvāpatti), non-attachment (asaṃsakti), non-perception of objects (padārthabhāvanā) and the fourth (turyagā); each is defined.

The stages are mapped onto the measures of Oṃ (a, u, m, half-measure, each gross, subtle, seed and witness); the first three are the seeker's, the fourth makes a knower of Brahman, the fifth the excellent, the sixth the more excellent, the seventh the most excellent knower.

In the first three stages the world is seen as in waking, in the fourth as in dream, in the fifth as in deep sleep; the sixth is like sleepiness within that; the seventh is deep sleep of the world entirely.
Marks of the one liberated in life: free of 'I' and 'mine', equal-minded, untouched by the body's experiences.

Two paths: Śuka's path of the bird (vihaṅgama), immediate liberation through inquiry into the great sayings; Vāmadeva's path of the ant (pipīlikā), gradual liberation over births through yoga — a haṭha practitioner hindered by obstacles or powers is reborn in a great family and continues. Both reach Brahman.
Mantra, laya and haṭha yoga suit practitioners of dull, middling and superior capacity.

The kuṇḍalinī lies in the triangle at the base; she is the supreme power from which breath, fire, bindu, nāda, haṃsa and mind arise; the six centres are the seat of Śakti, from the throat to the crown the seat of Śambhu.
Prāṇāyāma of knowledge: exhalation is the renunciation of all external objects, inhalation the scriptural knowledge, retention one's own realization.
The three knots are pierced by yoga and by the grace of guru and god, through saṃskāras of many births.
Four stages: ārambha (outer rites set aside, inner performed), ghaṭa, paricaya and niṣpatti (natural yoga, liberation while living).
Brahmā (Hiraṇyagarbha) asks Maheśvara about kaivalya; he is taught the path of the siddhas.
Some say knowledge alone suffices; it does not bring perfection. Knowledge without yoga cannot liberate; yoga without knowledge is incapable; the seeker should practise both.
Even the knower needs the yoga of the body; bodies are unripe (apakva) or ripened (pakva) by the fire of yoga.

The yogin's body, burnt by the fire of yoga, is unseen even by gods; other knowers are 'lumps of flesh' reborn again, who meet a siddha and become yogins; knowledge comes from yoga in one birth; there is no path beyond yoga.
Merely thinking 'I am liberated' does not liberate at once.
Mind is tied to prāṇa like a bird tied by a string; the only means is prāṇa. Partial knowledge brings great suffering; it is like crossing the ocean in an unbaked pot.
Yoga is the union of apāna and prāṇa, of rajas and retas, of sun and moon, of jīvātman and paramātman.

Mantra, laya, haṭha and rāja are four stages of one great yoga: mantra-yoga is the natural haṃsa repetition reversed as so'ham; haṭha the union of ha (sun) and ṭha (moon); laya the union of the knower of the field and the supreme; rāja the union of rajas and retas.
Two ways: the monkey's (gradual, completed in one body) and the crow's (the body perishes, he is reborn, meets a siddha guru and gains the fruit quickly).

Powers are of two kinds: contrived (from mercury, herbs, rites, mantras — impermanent and weak) and uncontrived (arising spontaneously, permanent, in those free of vāsanās); they are to be kept secret, like tīrthas seen on the way. As goldsmiths test gold, the siddha is known by his powers; one without powers is still bound.
Liberation is not the falling of the body; the yogin's body becomes Brahman like salt dissolved in water.
The body is Śiva's temple: ten doors, channels and winds; four seats (pīṭha) — Kāmarūpa at the mūlādhāra, Pūrṇagiri at the heart, Jālandhara at the throat, Uḍyāna between the brows.
This should be taught only to one who has served for twelve years.
Brahman has three bodies — gross (Vairāja), subtle (Hiraṇyagarbha, nāda) and supreme (being-consciousness-bliss); signs of the subtle are a lamp-flame, the moon, fireflies, lightning and stars.
There is no mantra higher than nāda, no god higher than one's own Self, no worship higher than inner attention (anusandhāna), no happiness higher than contentment.

original.text: nāsti nādāt paro mantro na devaḥ svātmanaḥ paraḥ | nānusandheḥ parā pūjā na hi tṛpteḥ paraṃ sukham

paraphrase: The power in the mūlādhāra as bindu sprouts as nāda (paśyantī), roars in the heart (madhyamā) and comes forth by the palate as vaikharī; from it arise letters, words, sentences, all mantras, Vedas, śāstras, purāṇas, poetry, languages and the seven notes; she is Sarasvatī; seeing her gives mastery of speech.
Non-dual teaching: the world is superimposed like a snake on a rope; one who makes even a little difference has fear.

Concentration on nāda gives far-hearing, on bindu far-seeing, on kāla knowledge of the three times, on another's body entry into bodies, on nectar freedom from hunger and poison, on the elements their mastery; bhāva is the cause.

The guru is Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Sadāśiva; there is no difference between guru and Lord; one should never argue non-duality against the guru, but contemplate with devotion the non-duality of guru, god and self.
The yogin should not set his mind on powers.
Of the 72,000 doors only the suṣumnā — the power of Śambhu — is useful; the others are useless.
Liberation comes if the guru himself is pleased; restraining the breath at the ādhāra the body trembles and the yogin dances.

The suṣumnā is praised as the supreme tīrtha — greater than Gaṅgā, Maṇikarṇikā, Śrīśaila, Vārāṇasī and Kedāra; a thousand horse-sacrifices are not worth a sixteenth of it; it is the supreme japa and meditation.
A moving mind is saṃsāra, a still mind liberation; the unmanī state is beyond merit and sin.
The mind looking at the mind: the ten signs (pratyaya) — bindu, nāda, kalā, light, sun, moon, pole-star, star, the peaceful and what is beyond — make him lord of yogins.
Attention to nāda destroys vāsanās; nāda is bindu, and bindu is mind.
Fire in wood appears by churning; the lamp in a pot shows when the pot breaks by the guru's word; the guru is the helmsman.
Vaiśravaṇa, son of Brahmā and a Vālakhilya, asks Svayambhū about the supreme; Oṃ's measures and the three deities — Rudra (tamas), Viṣṇu (sattva), Brahmā (rajas) — are explained.

Rudra-Paśupati is the doer of the inner sacrifice; its fire is the haṃsa 'so'ham', its thread the praṇava; attention to nāda is the rite; without meditation on haṃsa and praṇava there is no liberation.
Non-injury is the sacrifice of dharma; the paramahaṃsa is its priest.
Māyā exists only from the standpoint of empirical usage; in truth there is none.
Purity of food brings purity of mind; the knower sees 'I am the food and the eater'.
